title: Not alone in it
hook: Christians see in the cross a God who suffers with humanity

segments.voice: Yesterday: the garden at night, and a prayer that asked for the hard thing to be taken away. Your line was not as I will, but as thou wilt. Did you say out loud, to anyone, what you honestly wished? Today, the cup is not taken. Day seven hundred seventeen.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The garden prayer asked for the cup to pass. In Matthew's telling, it doesn't. Within hours there is an arrest, a trial before the high priest, a night of denials, and then a place called Golgotha. Christian teaching reads the cross in more than one way. Some readings ask what it paid for, or what it won. Today's reading asks something quieter. Who is on that cross, and which side of the pain is he standing on? Watching it from above, or inside it?
screen: `THE CUP DOES NOT PASS.` → `A PLACE CALLED GOLGOTHA.` → `WHICH SIDE OF THE PAIN?`

segments.voice: First, a name. In its first chapter, Matthew's Gospel gives a child the name Emmanuel, and it translates the name for its readers: "God with us." Not God above us, or God watching us. With. Second, the cross. Christians read the crucifixion through that name. In their telling, the one hanging there is not a stranger to pain watching it from far off. He is inside it: betrayed by a friend, deserted, beaten, mocked. And near the end, Matthew records him crying out with the opening line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's the King James wording. Even the feeling of being abandoned, in this reading, is a place he has been. Third, a letter. The Letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." A double negative, almost shy. It means he can be touched. He knows what weakness feels like from the inside. Fourth, how churches say it. Christians describe Christ's suffering in different words. Some theologians speak of God himself suffering on the cross. Others hold that the divine nature cannot suffer, and that the Son suffered truly in his human nature. Both are trying to keep hold of the same thing: on the cross, Christians say, God came into the worst of human pain, not only above it. The cup is not taken away. In this reading, it is drunk by someone on the inside of suffering, so that nobody in it is alone.
screen: `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · `INSIDE THE PAIN, NOT WATCHING IT.` · `TOUCHED WITH THE FEELING.` · `CHURCHES SAY IT DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind someone who is suffering right now. A friend, a parent, a neighbor, someone in the news. You don't need to fix anything. Breathing in, say their name silently. Breathing out, say: not alone. Keep that rhythm. If the mind starts drafting advice, let the draft go and come back to the name. Near the end, choose one small way to keep them company today: a message, a call, a visit. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Emmanuel, the name Matthew gives Jesus, meaning God with us, inside suffering and not only above it. Today's word.
Your line: he can be touched. Today, keep company with one person who is going through something hard. A message, a call, a chair pulled up. No advice needed. Day seven hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross, especially in Holy Week and on Good Friday, as the place where God shares human suffering, and visit the sick and grieving as a work of mercy.

fork.setup: you're reading Hebrews: "we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." what is the double negative saying?
options: he is kept far from human weakness.
he can be touched; he knows weakness from the inside.
fork.reveal: "not... cannot" means he can. Christians read it as a God who knows suffering from the inside, not from a distance.

original.note: Hebrew, from Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23 translates it: God with us.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross is only about something paid or settled.
what it means: Christians also see in it a God who comes into suffering, so that no one is in it alone.
what a scholar hears: Emmanuel in Matthew 1:23, the cry of Psalm 22 in Matthew 27:46, Hebrews 4:15, and an old debate over whether the divine nature can suffer.

notes: The two ways of speaking about Christ's suffering (God suffering on the cross vs. the divine nature being impassible and the Son suffering in his human nature) are given without ranking or attribution to named churches; a Keeper may want named examples or a softer summary.
'With the older creeds' refers loosely to the classical (Chalcedonian) tradition of divine impassibility; confirm the phrasing is fair.
Matthew 27:46 is the opening of Psalm 22; the script says 'the opening line of a psalm' without numbering it in voice. Confirm.
Practice and carry follow the outline (keep company with someone suffering).
